t: Valid Binary Strings With Cost Limit
o: We need every length-n binary string with no two adjacent '1's whose cost (sum of indices holding '1') is at most k. With n <= 12 there are at most 4096 strings, so exhaustive generation is trivially fast. In example 1 (n = 3, k = 1), of the five no-adjacent-ones strings, only 000, 010, 100 have cost <= 1. The no-adjacent-ones condition suggests either backtracking (decide each position, never placing '1' right after another '1') or iterating all 2^n masks and filtering.
k: n <= 12 means at most 2^12 = 4096 candidates, so brute-force enumeration is optimal in practice.
The no-consecutive-ones filter on a mask is a single bitwise test: mask & (mask << 1) == 0.
Backtracking prunes naturally: never place '1' after '1', and abandon branches whose cost already exceeds k.

a.i: Build the string left to right. At each position we may always place '0'; we may place '1' only if the previous character is not '1', adding the current index to the cost. Prune any branch whose running cost exceeds k.
s: Place '0' and recurse; if allowed, place '1' with cost += position and recurse.
At position n, record the string if cost <= k (guaranteed by pruning).
a.t: O(F * n) where F is the number of Fibonacci-like no-adjacent-ones strings (at most 2^n) — string building dominates.

a.i: Iterate all masks from 0 to 2^n - 1. Reject masks with adjacent set bits via (mask & (mask << 1)) != 0; otherwise compute the cost as the sum of set-bit indices and keep the mask if cost <= k. Simple, branch-free, and easy to reason about.
s: Skip if mask & (mask << 1) is nonzero (adjacent ones).
Compute cost = sum of indices of set bits; if cost <= k, convert the mask to a string and append.
a.t: O(2^n * n) — each of the 4096 masks is checked and converted in linear time.

w: Either approach passes instantly; bitmask enumeration is shorter and less error-prone, while backtracking demonstrates pruning and scales conceptually to larger n with the cost constraint. Pitfalls: the cost uses 0-based indices (index 0 contributes nothing, so leading '1's are free), and k = 0 admits strings whose ones sit only at index 0. Note the empty result is possible (e.g., n = 2, k = 0 forces only "00"... actually "00" qualifies, but n = 12, k = 0 yields exactly one string). A follow-up might ask to count valid strings instead of listing them — solvable with digit-style DP over (position, prevBit, cost).
